questions.questionText: What principle determines how much human oversight an AI system's action should have, according to this lesson?
options: Every single action should always require human approval, with no exceptions
The level of automation should match the reversibility and blast radius of the action — read-only actions can run autonomously, consequential ones need proportional human oversight
Human oversight is only needed for actions involving money
No AI system should ever have human oversight, it defeats the purpose of automation
questions.correctAnswer: The level of automation should match the reversibility and blast radius of the action — read-only actions can run autonomously, consequential ones need proportional human oversight
questions.explanation: This proportional approach — matching oversight to how hard an action would be to undo and how much damage it could cause — is the throughline from the Agentic AI course's human-in-the-loop lesson and this project's own operating guidelines.

questions.questionText: Why is evaluation described as an "ongoing practice" rather than a one-time pre-launch check?
options: Because evaluation is only useful before the very first launch
Because a model/prompt that worked well when last checked isn't guaranteed to keep working as data drifts, usage shifts, or upstream dependencies change
Ongoing evaluation is unnecessary once a system passes its initial eval set
Evaluation only matters for classification models, not LLMs
questions.correctAnswer: Because a model/prompt that worked well when last checked isn't guaranteed to keep working as data drifts, usage shifts, or upstream dependencies change
questions.explanation: This connects the MLOps monitoring lesson's point about silent degradation with the NLP/LLM course's eval-set discipline — quality can erode over time even without any code change, so evaluation needs to be continuous.

questions.questionText: Why does the responsible-deployment checklist recommend starting from the simplest adequate approach (e.g. prompting before fine-tuning)?
options: Simpler approaches always produce better raw performance
Simpler systems are easier to evaluate, secure, and reason about, which matters directly for responsible deployment, not just cost
Complex approaches are illegal to deploy
There is no reason, complexity should always be preferred
questions.correctAnswer: Simpler systems are easier to evaluate, secure, and reason about, which matters directly for responsible deployment, not just cost
questions.explanation: Beyond the cost argument from the fine-tuning lesson, simpler systems are more tractable to evaluate thoroughly and reason about for safety, which is itself a responsible-deployment consideration.
